title: Reducing the Stress of High-Density Living: An Architectural Intervention
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
article_family: environmental psychology; architectural psychology; crowding; residential stress

findings.antecedent: Long-corridor dormitory floor design (40+ residents sharing space)
findings.consequent: Residents report increased crowding stress and social problems
findings.statement: Long-corridor residents reported more crowding and residential social problems over time compared to those in shorter-corridor designs
findings.source: questionnaire data; observational period over semester
findings.quote: long-corridor residents reported more crowding and control-related problems

stimulus_description.mechanism: Increased group size and shared space

findings.mechanism: Reduced perceived control over shared spaces leads to stress and social withdrawal
theory_links: crowding-stress model (high density -> loss of control -> stress)

findings.antecedent: Architectural intervention: conversion of long-corridor floor to short-corridor design via physical barriers
findings.consequent: Reduced crowding stress, improved perceived control, increased group formation
findings.statement: The architectural modification (creating a long-corridor-intervention floor with physical separation) reduced crowding stress and control-related problems on the altered floor compared to the unaltered long-corridor floor
findings.quote: residents of the altered long-corridor floor reported fewer of these problems on the altered floor, whereas short-corridor residents (20 residents sharing space) did not change
findings.provenance_depth: primary data from controlled field study

scope_conditions.intervention: physical barriers creating smaller groups (~20 residents)

stimulus_description.intervention: Addition of barriers/doors in long-corridor to create smaller, more controllable groups

findings.mechanism: Reduced group size and increased boundary control enables better regulation of social contact and group formation
theory_links: group formation and control regulation theory

findings.antecedent: Perceived control in dormitory setting during initial orientation
findings.consequent: All three residential groups (long, long-intervention, short) report comparable initial levels of perceived control
findings.statement: During orientation, residents of all three environments reported comparable feelings of control in the dormitory
findings.quote: During orientation, residents of all three environments reported comparable feelings of control in the dormitory

findings.antecedent: Long-corridor design with loss of perceived control (week 5-10 of residence)
findings.consequent: Decreased ability to regulate social contact and increased stress symptoms
findings.statement: During the 5th and 12th weeks of residence, long-corridor residents reported less perceived control than did the other students, and more difficulty in regulating their social contact and less control in the dormitory and perceived dormitory life to be more hectic and less controllable
findings.quote: long-corridor residents reported increasing difficulties in regulating their social contact in the dormitory and perceived dormitory life to be more hectic and less controllable
findings.mechanism: Large group size impairs ability to regulate encounters with others and maintain personal control
theory_links: crowding as loss of control model

findings.antecedent: Long-corridor residents' feeling of loss of control in shared spaces
findings.consequent: Reported difficulty achieving small group formation on their floor
findings.statement: Long-corridor residents reported that small groups were less likely to form on their floor than did residents of the other floors
findings.quote: Long-corridor residents reported that small groups were less likely to form on their floor than did residents of the other floors
findings.source_zone: Results section, page 476, Group Formation subsection

stimulus_description.condition: Large shared floor vs. smaller clustered spaces

findings.mechanism: Large group size inhibits formation of intimate subgroups and social networks

findings.antecedent: Short-corridor and long-corridor-intervention floor designs with smaller residential groups
findings.consequent: Increased likelihood of small group formation compared to long-corridor
findings.statement: Residents of short-corridor and long-corridor-intervention floors reported being more successful in making friends or forming small groups on their floor than did residents of long-corridor floors
findings.quote: successful in making friends or forming small groups on their floor than on residents of intervention and short-corridor floors
findings.mechanism: Smaller group size facilitates interpersonal network formation and friendship development
theory_links: optimal group size for social cohesion

findings.antecedent: Long-corridor residents' knowledge of comparable neighbors during semester
findings.consequent: Fewer known neighbors as semester progresses (weeks 5 and 12)
findings.statement: Although residents of all three environments reported knowing comparable numbers of neighbors during orientation, long-corridor residents reported knowing fewer as friends after 5 and 12 weeks of residence
findings.quote: long-corridor residents reported knowing fewer as friends after 5 and 12 weeks of residence
findings.mechanism: Loss of control and stress in large groups impairs social bonding and network development

findings.antecedent: No significant difference in perceived crowding across residential groups at baseline
findings.consequent: By weeks 5-12, long-corridor residents report significantly higher crowding perception
findings.statement: There were no differences across residential groups for perceived crowding in the dormitory during orientation, but during the 5th and 12th weeks of residence, long-corridor residents felt more crowded in the dormitory than short-corridor residents
findings.quote: There were no differences across residential groups for perceived crowding in the dormitory during orientation, but during the 5th and 12th weeks of residence, long-corridor residents felt more crowded in the dormitory
findings.mechanism: Exposure to large group density over time increases subjective crowding perception

findings.antecedent: Observational assessment of hallway and social activity in long-corridor dormitory
findings.consequent: Significantly less social activity (2+ people interacting) compared to short-corridor and long-corridor-intervention settings
findings.statement: Less social activity (two or more people interacting) was observed in the long-corridor environment, F(2, 60) = 8.503, p < .001. These differences did not emerge immediately (see Figure 2); an interaction between residential group and length of residence indicated that clear differences were not found until the 10th week of residence
findings.source: observational data from 15-minute periods during weeks 3-15
findings.quote: Less social activity (two or more people interacting) was observed in the long-corridor environment
findings.source_zone: Results section, page 477, Observational Findings subsection
findings.mechanism: Loss of perceived control and crowding stress reduces voluntary social engagement in shared spaces
moderators_reported: length of residence (difference emerges at week 10)

findings.antecedent: Open bedroom doors as indicator of social availability in dormitory
findings.consequent: Long-corridor residents less likely to leave doors open; open doors decrease over time in long-corridor
findings.statement: Counts of open doors indicated that long-corridor residents were less likely to leave their doors open than were short-corridor or long-corridor-intervention residents, F(2, 60) = 19.193, p < .001. This was qualified by an interaction with length of residence (see Figure 3), F(18, 60) = 2.251, p < .01
findings.quote: long-corridor residents were less likely to leave their doors open than were short-corridor or long-corridor-intervention residents
findings.mechanism: Crowding stress leads to withdrawal and boundary control through physical barriers (closed doors)

findings.antecedent: Laboratory anagrams task performance under observation by confederate
findings.consequent: Long-corridor residents differ in anagram solving success and social approach behavior
findings.statement: Differences between residents of the long-corridor, short-corridor, and long-corridor-intervention floors were also evident in the laboratory. Three residents of each residential group were observed in the laboratory during the 5th through 11th weeks of dormitory residence
findings.quote: Three residents of each residential group were observed in the laboratory during the 5th through 11th weeks of dormitory residence
findings.source_zone: Results section, page 478, Laboratory Findings subsection
findings.mechanism: Crowding effects on task performance and social behavior persist in laboratory settings
theory_links: environmental stress effects on cognitive performance
transfer of social anxiety across contexts

findings.antecedent: Long-corridor resident seating proximity to confederate during waiting
findings.consequent: Long-corridor residents sit farther away from confederate (greater interpersonal distance)
findings.statement: Long-corridor resident (excepting the 9th) and their behavior in the laboratory was consistent with previous findings that long-corridor residents persist in avoiding contact by assuming more withdrawn postures than those of intervention and short-corridor floors
findings.quote: Long-corridor resident...persist in avoiding contact by assuming more withdrawn postures

stimulus_description.situation: seated waiting for experiment with confederate in adjacent location

findings.mechanism: Crowding-induced withdrawal and social avoidance behaviors generalize to new laboratory settings

findings.antecedent: Long-corridor resident facial regard toward confederate waiting partner
findings.consequent: Less facial regard; longer latency to look at confederate's face
findings.statement: Long-corridor residents expected to have less eye contact and less control, long-corridor residents looked at her less often, F(2, 52) = 4.620, p < .01 and felt more uncomfortable following the 5-minute waiting period
findings.quote: Long-corridor residents looked at her less often
findings.mechanism: Crowding-induced social avoidance manifests as reduced visual attention to others

findings.antecedent: Long-corridor resident discomfort after 5-minute laboratory waiting period with confederate
findings.consequent: Reported greater discomfort and less willingness to interact further
findings.statement: Long-corridor residents reported more discomfort in the waiting situation than those of intervention and short-corridor floors, F(2, 61) = 37.82, p < .001 (see Table 2). They more strongly agreed with the statement, 'It is often not worth the effort to try to change the way things are' than did residents of intervention and short-corridor floors, F(2, 61) = 44.05, p < .001
findings.quote: Long-corridor residents reported more discomfort in the waiting situation
findings.mechanism: Crowding stress produces learned helplessness and reduced motivation to engage with others

findings.antecedent: Long-corridor resident expectancy for control in laboratory setting
findings.consequent: Expected less control, looked less, and reported less willingness to engage compared to other groups
findings.statement: Long-corridor residents expected to have less control over the session once it started (did diffter from other groups, F(2, 52) = 7.180, p < .01. No other differences among residential groups were found for behavior or mood in the waiting situation
findings.quote: Long-corridor residents expected to have less control over the session
findings.mechanism: Chronic exposure to crowding stress and loss of control generalizes as expectancy for control deficits in new situations

limitations: Study conducted in single college dormitory setting; generalizability to other high-density residential settings unknown
Single semester observation period; long-term effects beyond one academic year not examined
Small sample size for laboratory portion (n=3 per group)
Randomly assigned residents; not clear how self-selection would affect findings in naturalistic settings
Alternative explanations for differences (e.g., Baron & Mandel, 1978) were not ruled out
Effect of length of residence could not separate from possible cohort effects
overall_theory_links: Baum & Valins (1977) architectural mediation model: design features moderate crowding stress through effects on group size and control
High-density behavioral model: loss of perceived control is primary mechanism by which density produces stress
Environmental determinism: physical environment directly shapes social behavior and stress responses
Crowding-stress sequential model: effects of density accumulate over time, with behavioral withdrawal following initial stress phase
Withdrawal behavior model: crowding leads to avoidance, reduced group formation, and social isolation as coping mechanisms
